titleStmt.title: Interview with Andre G. Beaumont, Undated
titleStmt.author: Thomas J. Healy II

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Andre G. Beaumont was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, you've got to remember when you're telling me, when you're answering me --

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- the only person they're going to hear is you.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So if I ask you a question, sort of start out with the question, then the answer to it. In other words, so you're going to hear, like -- A perfect thing is, like, okay, like, were you in D-day -- and I don't know whether you were at D-day -- but in D-day, usually people say yes and will stop, and people don't know what you're saying yes to.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: So, in other words, I have to say --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you say, "I participated in D-day." If I say, "Did you participate, you know, were you in D-day?" "Yes, I participated in D-day" and go on with it. Or I'm going to ask you a series of questions right now that are just basically who, what, when, and where of, like, where did you grow up --

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- who were your parents, and what did they do --

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- and then did you have any brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Uh-hmm, uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then you can continue on in that, the fact of I grew up wherever; my parents bup-bup-bup, whatever; I have so-and-so brothers and sisters; I attended high school at such-and-such a high school or I graduated in such, and I went on to college, whatever. So you can continue those three questions anytime you want. So I'm going to ask you, which we'll start with, where did you grow up?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: I grew up in New York City, and my parents were immigrants from Europe. My father was French. My mother was Swiss. And I grew up speaking French as my first language. But I went to school in New York, and actually I was born in New York, so -- but I was born after they came to the country obviously. And by the time I graduated from high school, which was 1943, the war, we had been in the war for already two years. And I was accepted to Harvard in June of '43, and at that time they were running 12 months a year. So I was in from June of '43 until about February of '44. And what I did, they used to draft you -- I turned 18 in January, January 3rd of '44, and I wanted to at least finish my freshman year at Harvard. And the army had a program that you could enlist, and they wouldn't call you up until your semester was over. So I enlisted in December of '43 in the army, and I was called up middle of March, which allowed me to finish my first year at Harvard.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. I forgot to start out with this, but give me your full name, and then spell your last name.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: My full name is Andre G. Beaumont, and it's spelled B-e-a-u-m-o-n-t.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So you got out of Harvard. Okay. Here's the next big question. December 7th. And what I'd like you to do is say December 7th, 1941, I was playing marbles out back; I was drinking beer at whatever. So where were you December 7th, 1941, and what do you remember of Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: December 7th, 1941, I will not forget. I was at that time 15 years old, and we were at home, and we -- in our apartment in Manhattan and listening to the radio. And I think the symphony was on. And the broadcast was interrupted by an announcement that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor, which was somewhat of a -- It was obviously a big shock. But my parents, having been in Europe during World War I and when the war started in 1939, they had premonitions that we were going to get into the war at one time or another. And unfortunately they were right. But I was still a little bit too young to know really what this was going to mean for me, because I was only 15 years old. I did have -- I did have a brother -- he's now deceased -- who was a half brother. He was 18 years older than I was. He was born in France. And he was called up by, when he was 18, by the French government to serve his one year of military training. Then he came to live in the United States. And he was living with us at the time of 1939. He received a letter from the French Embassy saying he has to report for active duty in the French Army. And he says I -- you can't call me up because I'm a United States citizen now. So he thought he was sitting fine. They passed the draft law in 1940, and he was one of the first ones drafted in the American Army. But, anyway, so he was already in the military when Pearl Harbor came. Actually he had written us a letter to tell us that he was going to be discharged in December of '41 because he had fulfilled over a year of service. And obviously that was changed quickly.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Rescinded?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Rescinded, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So tell me a little bit about when you -- once you finally finished your first year at Harvard and you went in in March, where did you report to, what kind of training did you have, what did you do? And then we'll stop there. And then we'll, once you've finished all that, then how did you get over to wherever you were and all that. So if you could just start with --

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: When I was called up for active duty in March -- because what you did, you enlisted, and they put me in Reserve Corps, and then I was called up for active duty in March. I reported to Fort Dix, New Jersey. And Fort Dix was a huge induction center, they called it. And I don't know how many -- I would assume almost a thousand men a day showed up there to be processed into the Army. And it was like a mass production operation where you were both medically examined, screened, take intelligence tests, get your shots, get your uniforms, and all that. And from there I was sent to Georgia, to Camp Stewart, Georgia. It's now Fort Stewart. It's right outside of Savannah. It was an anti-aircraft training center. And I was being trained in a 90mm anti-aircraft gun battery. And they selected me and a couple of other guys. I think what they looked at was the scores we made on the intelligence tests. And they put us in the director section. Now, I learned how to be a gunner and to do all the stuff to set up the guns and fire it and all that. But at the same time they trained us in running this big Sperry gyroscope mechanical computer, which took in information as far as the altitude, elevation, left, right, all the different factors. And it factored in wind and moisture. It was fairly sophisticated, which tracked the planes, the target, and fed information to the guns. And so we did that, and I graduated from that, went home for a week leave of absence, returned to Camp Stewart. And then after about a week or two, I was shipped to Camp Hahn, California. That was a five-day train trip. And we arrived in Camp Hahn, which is right outside of Riverside. Actually I think there's still March Field there. March Field is the big airbase. And Camp Hahn was across the way from March Field. And that was also an anti-aircraft camp. And I was assigned to a 90mm gun battalion. And I was assigned to the director section. The only thing is they had a brand new electronic Western Electric director that sat in an air-conditioned trailer, and the lieutenant in charge of the directions had his electric razor. It was a very classy operation. While these guys were outside firing these guns, I was in this nice, little, air-conditioned trailer. And we were supposed to go to the Pacific, and that made it even better, because -- my goodness, that's wonderful -- going to be in these tropical islands in an air-conditioned trailer. But that didn't last long. The whole camp was disbanded, which was about, I imagine, around October -- September or October of '44. And every unit -- and it made no difference whether you were radar, specialist, or what you were -- everybody was sent to infantry training. And we were trained as -- We had a six-week hurry-up course to be trained as infantry replacements. And so that was the end of my anti-aircraft career, and I found myself in Texas. We'd get up at 4:00 in the morning, full field packs, gas masks, steel helmets, everything, five hours -- five miles out, and then we'd have breakfast. And then we'd maneuver in the field all day. They'd feed us lunch out in the field. And then we'd march back, have dinner, and go to bed very early and up the crack of dawn. It was quite a -- I was in great shape when I got through that, because, I mean, we had -- Well, we did physical education, you know, all these exercises and stuff out in the field. And then we were shipped across the country to Fort Meade, Maryland. Maryland, that was a big processing center to be sent overseas. And we turned in all our equipment, sent all our personal property home, anything that was our personal goods. And we then got all brand new stuff that we had never seen before. It was all equipment that was really new design, new color, everything, because most -- I think most of the stuff that I had while we were in training was really sort of a hangover from World War I. It may have not been made for World War I, but it was still the same design, pattern, and so forth, the packs and everything. So we spent about three days there, I think. We got new -- Everything had to be marked with your first letter and your last name and your last three numbers of your serial number. And we had every single thing, socks, underwear, everything, had this. And my number was 11133284, and so my thing was B3284. Everything was indelible, and even the gas mask. Anyway, this was great, I guess. And we were put on a train, and they -- with our steel helmets on, and they put numbers on our head. And I couldn't figure out what this was for. On our steel helmet they wrote this. And I couldn't figure out what this was for, because the usual pattern was you go from Fort Meade, Maryland, to some camp in New Jersey, and from thence you went to New York, where you shipped out to Europe. Well, in our shipment -- and they told us that we were a new process -- we went directly from Fort Meade, Maryland, to a ferry dock in New Jersey. We actually pulled into a station there and unloaded, and we had to unload all of the numbers that we had on our helmets. And we marched through this ferry terminal, and there was, like, a little fence. And on the other side were all the civilians and commuters that were going across the river to Manhattan. And we got on a ferry boat, went across, and there was the Queen Elizabeth. Queen Elizabeth was the biggest and the fastest. It had never been used for civilian service. It was not completed in time. And so it was a troop transport. And they had about 16,000 men on that thing. And we got off, got -- marched on the ferry boat, got off the ferry boat, marched from the ferry boat, and they check you off. And as you board the boat, a Red Cross girl gives you a little packet with an orange, a candy bar, a little -- some kind of a western paperback novel, and good luck, buddy. So we got on this big boat, and I swear we got on the bottom, and we were way down. I could think, the torpedo, that was it, baby. We were way down at the bottom of the ship. And six deep these bunks were. And we were told immediately to put on a life vest, and we were given a big badge with a color and a number. And you had to stay within that area of the boat. I guess they didn't want everybody running to one side. It would tip the boat over. But whatever it was, we were restricted, and we also had assigned eating hours. But when we sailed out of Manhattan, everybody was brought up on decks, and our position on the deck was on the starboard front. So I was lucky. I got there, and I was able to see the Statue of Liberty as we pulled out of the harbor. And, anyway, I went down, ate. The next day I got -- Every morning we had to get up on the deck. And the next day I got up there, and I started looking around where are the escorting destroyers? Nothing. Nothing. We were by ourselves zigzagging. Needless to say, I got seasick, and it lasted for about a day or so. And then one day -- I guess it took us about four, five days to cross -- and we arrived in the Firth of Clyde in Scotland. And it was a beautiful, clear January -- early January day. And there was Scottish highlands coming up on both sides. And the water was just flat and beautiful. And we sailed down there. And two RAF Spitfires came and flew over us, and they waggled their wings, and it was a great, great sight. And we unloaded in Greenock, also ferry boats. And one of the interesting things on the ferry boats, as we landed, one of my classmates from Harvard, who -- they kept on bugging me and everybody __+ a year of college, okay, go to OCS. So I said, yeah, I'll go to OCS for coast artillery, which is anti-aircraft. They said, oh, no, infantry or tank corps or artillery. I said no way. Artillery means that you were a forward observer, second lieutenant. A guy comes way up there. And so I said no, no, I'm not going to be a -- Well, my buddy decided he was going to be a -- he went to OCS. I saw this guy. He was on the upper decks with all these second lieutenants. It was my classmate from Harvard, was way up there, and I was down here with all the mass of the troops and the -- All I could do was wave at him, yell, "Hey, Jack. Hey, Jack. Hey, Jack." Well, anyway, he got killed in February of that year. He was obviously leading his -- I'm sure he was a damn good lieutenant, but he didn't last long. He couldn't have lasted more than about a month and a half from that time I was there. Anyway, we got off this ferry in Greenock, and Greenock is a small port there up the river from Glas -- up the firth from Glasgow. We got on these troop trains, and they shot us through England. We stopped once, and these ladies fed us meat pies and coffee. And we went on and got off in South Hampton, where we walked off the trains and got on a boat that was, I guess, a converted freighter. It was run by Sikhs. And these are guys that must be about -- They seemed like they were seven-foot tall. They had these turbans. And they had these curved knives stuck in their belt. They looked absolutely fearsome, ferocious-looking guys. But they were very nice guys. And we slept in hammocks. That was the only time in my life I ever slept in a hammock. They had these -- You went in this -- It was a cargo area, and they had all these poles, and there was hammocks. And you had to sleep on a hammock. Got off the -- Anyway, we arrived in Le Havre, and we again marched off the boat, got on a train. And they had these freight cars. They were forty and eights. They were called forty and eights, and I thought they were for forty men and eight horses. But when we got in there, they put thirty of us in there. I said they couldn't get eight horses and forty men in here. So finally somebody straightened me out many years later. It's forty men or eight horses. Anyway, we got on this, and they threw in a blanket, a blanket for every man. And we stopped somewhere on the way, this train, and finally they unloaded us somewhere in Belgium. And they took us on trucks to a place that had a chateau up on a hill. And we were down in the sort of a field opposite from the chateau. And we slept in tents. And there were no cots. We slept on the ground, and the ground was solid ice. So the best thing you could do is put the blankets underneath you. And we had sleeping bags. I slept in the sleeping bag with blankets underneath. And we went to the chateau to eat. I think we were there for one day, and they stuck us in a truck. And there were eight men in the truck. We arrived at this little village in Belgium and got off the truck and lined up. And the captain comes up: "I'm Captain Thomas Mitchell. Welcome to Company F, 331st Infantry, 83rd Infantry Division. We are just a mile or so from combat. We just came out of combat. We're going back in in a couple of days. And you men are first replacements. And go see the supply sergeant." Supply sergeant, they took everything that we had so carefully marked. Everything was taken away, including the gas mask. I mean, the only thing that we kept on was long underwear, wool pants, and a -- and the fatigue pants on top. So we had three layers of clothing, field jacket, sweater, which I had, and gloves we kept. By the way, by the time we were one of the last outfits on that Queen Elizabeth, they hadn't issued us rifles. We had no rifles. So we arrived, and we still had no rifles. We arrived at this rifle company, infantry unit, didn't have a rifle. But they had rifles, but they were all beat up. And so that was my introduction to Company F and the infantry.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That was January of --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- '45, so it was after D-day?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Yes, after D -- We were -- Yes, they were in the Battle of the Bulge. We arrive -- I arrived as a replacement in Belgium, and they were -- The 83rd Division was on the northern sector of what they call the Bulge. And actually it was under the -- It was in first army -- First Army had been transferred to the command of Montgomery's Army group. And our job was to, well, I guess, first of all, to contain the German invasion in the Bulge, the northern part of the Bulge, and then to push them back out. And that was, in January, that was what we were in the process of doing. And the Germans were, at that time, were still very potent. They were very good in retreating. And there were almost as many casualties in the January phase as in December. Maybe not as much. It certainly was not as tragic. The American units were overrun, and a lot of prisoners were taken at the beginning of the Battle of the Bulge. But my division had landed. The 83rd had landed I think it was like D plus 14, and they relieved the 101st Airborne that had parachuted in on D-day. And so they had fought in Normandy. They had fought in Brittany. They had fought through France into Luxembourg. And they had also -- One of the worst campaigns they had was in the Hurtgen Forest, none of which I participated in, but saw my first indoctrination with -- at the -- in the Battle of the Bulge in Belgium.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So you got there. You got all your rifle and everything handed to you.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How many days after that did you go into battle, and then what were you thinking about before that? I mean, were you anticipating that? Did you really give a shit? Did you whatever?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Well, I really, when I arrived there and I was, you know, issued my rifle, there were eight of us, and we were assigned to the third platoon, and I found out that -- the third squad of the third platoon, and I found out that was -- all that was left was the platoon sergeant. Well, he had two -- three squads. But the third squad only had the squad leader, who was a sergeant, plus one or two men. And it turned out that the -- we were filling in for some guys that had been literally slaughtered in some kind of an ambush two days before. And it is written up in our division history that this -- they were ambushed, and most of the men were also replacements, and they didn't know what to do. And their sergeants tried to get them to move, but they were mostly killed or wounded. And the sergeant pretended he was dead, because they actually -- the Germans came out and literally killed all the guys that were wounded that were lying in the snow. I should say, if it's not known, that that winter was one of the coldest in the history of Europe, and the snow was everywhere obviously. But the main thing was the cold. It was really bitter, bitter, terribly cold. So, anyway, we were assigned to this platoon, and I guess it was about the next day they took us out somewhere where we could fire our rifles to see if they worked. And then we started going out on patrols probing to find where there were Germans. And I really didn't -- you were so -- I guess you were so numbed fighting the cold, thinking of the cold, that it was -- you didn't know where -- you didn't know where the Germans were. You didn't know when you would find them or anything. You had no idea. We just -- We'd go out in a group of usually a squad or so of men.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How many is a squad?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Squad is about 12 men. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Which -- It's the squad. Then it's the platoon?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Platoon is next. There are three squads in a platoon, and there are three platoons in a rifle company. There's three rifle platoons, and then there's a weapons platoon, which has the 60mm mortars and the light machine guns.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So the patrols you were going out on were typically how many men?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Small groups. Well, in our -- And we only had ten men when I was there in our squad. And it would be -- There usually, though, was an officer that would go along. Usually the platoon commander, who was a lieutenant, would go along. And the idea was to go out until you drew fire. And you were not supposed to really engage the enemy. You were supposed to try to figure out where they were and then come back, and, you know, then he would report what we saw. And, well, we really -- so we really were not in firefights where we were trying to respond and overcome the enemy. And so we would come back, and he would report this. And then I imagine another company or another part of our company would then assault this particular position that we had scouted. That was the main function during the Battle of the Bulge. It was -- And we were -- Well, we had -- Either we went into holes in the ground at night or we went -- when we could find a barn or some kind of a building. I really have -- It's very vague because it was so -- it was so fast. But I do remember finally, I think, somewhere towards the end of January we pulled back, and we went into Belgium into some little village. And there we really sort of trained. I would say that during the time that I was there during the Battle of the Bulge, we had maybe, in our little squad, we maybe had one or two casualties. All I can remember is of the eight men that I came with, by the time the war was over, four of them had been killed, three of them had been wounded, and I was the only one that was neither wounded nor killed. Now, why that happened, I don't know, but after our time in Belgium, we went back into -- more into central -- into Germany, and we crossed the Ruhr River, and we attacked a bunch of German cities and towns. And it was the only time in my entire experience as a rifleman that we were briefed. We were told we were going to attack this town called Loveling. We were told that there would be artillery support. We were told that there were going to be trenches and barbed wire and that we would have resistance from not only the soldiers but the civilians and so on and so forth. We went to bed, and they told us that we would -- we had dinner, went to bed early, and -- well, bed -- sleep in your sleeping bag on the floor somewhere. We were in some -- I don't know -- some building somewhere. And we were told that they'd wake us up at 3:00 in the morning, and we would be attacking at 5:00. And I says it's going to be a rough fight and so on and so forth. So I went -- And I couldn't sleep. I was shivering. I was really afraid this was going to be it, because this was going to be really -- We were attacking a German town defended by Germans in their homeland and so forth. And they made it sound really very, very frightening. And, well, 3:00 came. We weren't awakened. Finally they woke us up around 6:00, threw breakfast at us, and got us in trucks. And we got off the trucks, and we got on these tanks. They were brand new Sheridan tanks. I had never seen these tanks before. And we passed through this battery of self-propelled 105mm Howitzers that were firing. And then we got into this field, and the tanks spread out, and you could see there was this town down here that was being shelled. It was quite a display, because they were firing white phosphorus, which just looks like a piece of fireworks. It's this white stuff. And it supposedly sets fire to everything that it hits, and -- I don't know -- there weren't too many fires when we got in there. But I was --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What kind of day was it, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: It was a cloudy -- It was a late February day. It was not bad, nothing compared to the Bulge. It was a cloudy day and dark. It was early morning, no sun. But it was -- At least there was no rain or snow. But the funny thing is, one of my funny experiences, one of the things they issued us I kept hand grenades strapped onto my little -- we had, like, suspenders to hold our cartridge belts, which were full of clips of eight rounds each for the M1 rifle. We had a hand grenade taped to each side here, and I had a -- They gave us a quarter pound of TNT, which you also taped onto a little open part of your cartridge belt. To detonate the TNT, you had a little fulminate of mercury detonator, which is a little copper thing with a fuse, and you could light that with a match, or there was some places they had little fuse igniters. And one of the guys, when I got this, I said, "Where do I put this?" He said, "It's very sensitive, so put it as far away from the TNT as you can, because it will set off the TNT." So he said, "Why don't you put it in the back." And I have a first aid packet in the back of my pants of my cartridge -- my cartridge belt was hooked on, a little rectangular thing you've probably seen or heard of. And so I says, "Put it in there." So I had this thing sitting in back here. I never thought about it, anyway, for quite awhile. We had it in Belgium, had it through the time we were in Germany. So I'm sitting on the back of this tank, and all of a sudden there's an explosion, and I'm thrown off the back of the tank. I said, "What the hell? I've already been hit, and I haven't even done anything." And, you know, it was this thing that had exploded in my -- because we were sitting on top of the motor, the back of the tank. It was warm. Anyway, so everybody laughed, and I couldn't -- I -- Yeah. So I got back on the tank, and finally we got out, and the tanks fired over our heads, and we charged into the town. We, a few times, we up and down, and we found a nest of Germans that were shooting at us. And yeah, they were, yeah, the billets were (imitating sound). I think there was one that I felt the heat from the damn thing. But we did spot this nest, and we fired with our rifles into this corner. Yes, sir? (Pause for interruption.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Okay. Well, anyway, we did -- and we asked -- Each squad has a BAR man, Browning automatic rifle. And we asked the BAR man to spray that building. And eventually we got into the town, and we had some -- There were, you know, no fortifications. There were no trenches. There was no barbed wire. There was no ferocious resistance. We had people that were resisting us. We had a few places where people were shooting at us. We were able to shoot back. And we had a sauerkraut factory where we went in. There was all these concrete bins. And there were German soldiers that were firing at us from in there. And we put in some mortar rounds. They went through the roof. And also we threw some hand grenades in there and finally cleared it out. And I remember there was a dead German in a batch of sauerkraut, a pickled German soldier, not a very happy fellow, although I like sauerkraut to this day. Anyway, we -- we cleaned out that town. And the next -- We didn't even stay the night. We stayed there for -- I guess we had meals. We didn't eat -- We ate C-rations. One of the things you do when you, in combat, you always have K-rations, these boxes. You'd stick them under your field jacket. So we had K-rations. And then we immediately set off into the -- at night, and we went across some fields. And then we got into a little bit of high ground, and we dug in. And one of the places that our squad where -- we were dug in in the direction from which we had come. I couldn't understand that and only found out later on that we had been cut off from the rest of our units and that we were literally an island. We were, say, we were surrounded, but we weren't being attacked, at any rate. But we were in the secure position on high ground, but we were cut off from our other units. But fortunately, I guess, sometime the next day, the communications were restored. But we went into the City of Neuss, which is across the Rhine River from Düsseldorf. And we cleared out several buildings, and there was tanks were shooting at each other. Off to our right and off -- further off was the Rhine River. And we finally ended up I was posted with a bunch of guys in a corner store at a bake shop in a big square. And they -- we set up a machine gun in there. One of our machine gunners came in there. And we were sort of an outpost. And we stopped there. We had cleared out this area, and we were there. And we were there for about almost a day in this bake shop. And the German civilians were in a bomb shelter right across the square from us. And we kept on telling them to stay in the shelter because there was still shooting going on out there. And we were not shooting at anyone at the time. Nobody was shooting at us. But there was still some shooting you could hear, and there was tanks. But, anyway, finally it settled down, and somebody from the bake shop came, and they offered us cookies and stuff, which I didn't want to eat. I was afraid it was going to be poisoned. So that was -- So then we moved into buildings on the Rhine, along the Rhine River. Our mortar people were firing mortars in there, and machine gunners were firing across the Rhine. They pulled us back. After several days we were relieved by the 104th Infantry Division. And then we trained in Holland on river crossings. And we did paddling these little boats, about eight men, plywood things, four men on each side paddling away. And we thought, well, we're going to cross the Rhine like this. Well, it didn't happen. We got in trucks, and we crossed the Rhine on a pontoon bridge. But we had -- we captured a number of towns without too much resistance, but we still took some casualties. But my -- the biggest fight was in the City of Hamm, H-a-m-m. And, oh, by that time I should say I was, quote-unquote, promoted. I had, from a rifleman, I was promoted to a radioman in company headquarters. We had three SCR-300 radios, which were FM radios. They weighed about 40 pounds. They were the only effective radio that we had. You'd probably seen these handy-talkies. They were literally worthless. They were AM radio, staticky, had a very short range. So 90 percent of the time they were ineffectual. But the 300 radio was FM, much more powerful, and was effective. So I was one of I think there were six of us in this communications squad that was part of company headquarters. And we carried these radios on our back. We were either assigned to the assault platoon or patrols or -- There was always one guy was with the captain at company headquarters. But on this particular day at Hamm, I was picked by the executive officer. We were going to go scout. We crawled through bushes and went up into, I guess, towards the -- where the enemy was shooting at us. They were shooting at us across the river with 88mm guns, and the -- We went, just the two of us, went up, and we found a farmhouse. And we went up to the top floor of the farmhouse where he could actually see with his binoculars where some of the German gun positions were. And he said, "Okay. Transmit this." So I set up to transmit. It wouldn't transmit. We had two antennas. We had a short, flexible antenna, and then we had a telescoping antenna, and it was about -- I don't know -- about 10 feet tall, a really very tall thing. So I said try the biggest. So I put the big antenna in, stuck the thing out the window, and started to transmit. And I don't think we transmitted more than two words before an 88 blasted the roof off this damn house. So we threw ourselves down the stairs, and the house was leveled by the time we got -- An 88, I don't know if you've heard about them, but they were the best guns the Germans had. They were anti-aircraft guns, but they used them for anti-tank and anti-personnel. They were very high velocity weapons. And you couldn't do -- Like, artillery, you could hear the thing (imitating sound) coming, and you could hit the ground. With this, it goes (imitating sound). It's almost instantaneous that you have the explosion. And they were using them for anti-personnel. And one of my best buddies was killed there. He was a squad member that came in with me. I still keep in touch with his family in North Dakota -- or South Dakota. Anyway, that morning he had pulled me around in my sleeping bag. We were sleeping on the floor of a German bar. And he come in and seen me and pulled me around. And we horsed around. And then I came back, and I found he had been -- head was blown off with an 88 explosion. But, anyway, so that was one of my happy experiences with the 88s. But the lieutenant and I got back in time. But we -- That town was a rail center. It was loaded with German flat cars with trucks. And our company, our whole, really, division, I guess, secured all these trucks. And we became a motorized division. And we moved with the Second Armored Division on our left and our -- I guess each company was assigned a certain territory. And we had a couple of Quartermaster trucks that were assigned to us. And we would -- then started what the newspaper people called the Ragtag Circus. We just -- We covered 30, 40 miles a day going into Germany. We would -- We had a German-speaking officer with us who we would go to a town, and he would go in under a flag of truce and ask for the Burgermeister and said, "Will you surrender your town to us?" And most of the time they did, and we would just drive through this town, and people would have white bedsheets hanging around. (Intercom interruption: Hello.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yes. (Intercom interruption: Your appointment's here.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Okay. We're practically finishing up. So we -- If they didn't, we would just fire a few .50 caliber rounds, and eventually they'd surrender. And we just drove through these towns. People would be standing on the street shocked, shocked that we were there. They couldn't believe it. Finally we reached the Elbe River, and we there got those little wooden boats and paddled across the Elbe River and made an assault crossing. We were fired on, machine gun fire, light machine gun fire, and some artillery, not too much, although the artillery did hit us while we were waiting to load the boats. One shrapnel hit one of our jeeps, which was full of -- had a trailer, Jeep trailer, full of mortar ammunition. And the cover, canvas cover, caught fire. So everybody beat that thing out, or else all of this mortar ammunition would have exploded. But anyway we crossed the Elbe River, and we marched I guess it would be towards the east. And we then dug in, set up a defensive position on the right flank of the bridge head. And we were there just one night. We did have a patrol of Germans that came, and they were all eliminated. And then we kept on hearing all this artillery and machine gun firing. And this was a typical infantry move. We said, okay, pick up and march. And I had my radio, and I was assigned to go with the captain. And we were marching along, and all of a sudden we hit these woods, and the sound of the gunfire gets louder and louder. And he says, okay, spread out, and we go through these woods, and they attacked this town. And that was it, you know. So -- And I went with the captain, and we did assault this town. And we were pinned down in the middle of the field by two machine gun fire, cross fires, one on either side. And we -- Fortunately there was a ditch with water in it, ice water, but it was better than being shot. And we radioed for the tank to fire over -- well, tried to spot these machine gunners. And they did. And, well, we marched into the town. The other platoon, I think, was sent around to the flank, and they came in that way. We had an interesting little thing. One of my buddies was assigned to march back some German prisoners to the rear, and he was -- he had been, like me, pinned down in this ditch of water. And we were really up to, ice cold water, almost up to the waist. So he made the prisoners march through a ditch of ice cold water on the way back. After that, we dug in, and we sat -- we did have one attack that was just -- I don't know -- end of April. We kept on -- We kept on looking for red flares from the Russians, because we were across the Elbe River but 60 miles from Berlin. But we sat -- We were told to stop, we dug in, and we had all these defensive positions. We had one attack --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Want some water?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Hmm?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Want some water?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: No. I'm fine. Anyway, we -- That was a really -- a very tragic thing, because we were attacked by -- they were either cadets -- Somebody said that they were naval cadets. There were all these young guys. And unfortunately they got in a situation where they were in kind of a gully, and they were pinned down by a machine gun. So if they got up, they were hit by machine gun. But they were in this gully. And they were perfect targets for mortars. And we must have -- Well, we had to call on the radio for more mortar ammunition, because they were just pouring 60mm mortar shells into that gully. And I don't know how many were killed or wounded in that, but that was -- that was really the last major action. And then we went back down through -- We had the -- well, one of the things were refugees. After the fighting was really major -- was over, and before the end of the war, the refugees started to pour through. They didn't want to be taken over by the Russians. And they couldn't -- We wouldn't let them use our bridge, the pontoon bridges. They were built for American vehicles. And, anyway, we retreated from there, seceded the ground to the Russians. We went through a couple of towns and finally ended up in Bavaria, where we started -- we got reequipped, retrained for the -- Japan. We were supposed to be one of the divisions in the assault on Japan. And we were loading up the trucks to go on maneuvers in Grafenwoehr, which is a big German training area. And as -- before we loaded up, the captain came out and told us "The war is over, guys. We're not going to maneuver." So then we just sat there for a while. Then I was transferred --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Was that V --

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: VE.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- VE-day?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: VE-day, yeah, that was VE-day. No, no, no. VJ-day. VJ-day. That was -- VE-day was in May.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And where were you then?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: That was -- I was sitting in the fields in -- across the Elbe River.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, okay. All right. That's where you're talking about. And then that happened.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: After VE-day, we retreated from the territory which was all ceded to the Russians. And we went down to Bavaria, which was going to be the American zone. And that's where we trained for Japan. And then that was where we learned that the war was over in Japan --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: August.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: -- in August and that we were going to go home. But I wasn't going home, because we had about 6 million men in Europe, and I was too young. And although I had three battle stars -- I had Battle of the Bulge, Central Europe, the Rhineland -- I was too young, and they transferred me to a post office unit in Munich, Germany. And the bunch of us were all these young guys. We were all -- what? -- we were 19 years old, and the guys that were running the post office, they seemed like they were 90 years old. They were about 35, 40 years old, but they were real post office employees. They had been drafted, and they were running army postal units. Anyway, we learned in about, I think, two weeks how to run a post office. And all these older guys went home. And so we lived in Munich. We lived in apartments. We had a maid service that cleaned and made our beds. We got in a truck. We went to a little restaurant where we were served Army food prepared by German cooks that was delicious. And we were served by Polish waitresses. And we had an orchestra that played at lunch and dinner. This was some kind of a -- They call it some kind of a mess. It was not an officers' mess. So that was a very lovely life. And that was where I was finally promoted to sergeant. I had Tech 4, which is sergeant. And I was the administrative sergeant for the post office, although I could do the whole -- We all learned to do the whole thing, how to sort mail, how to write money orders, sell stamps, and, you know, keep your cash boxes and all that stuff. It was a very nice life. And then from then I was shipped back to the United States, saw the Statue of Liberty again, and got off on Staten Island. That's my story.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What a great story. Now, you got back home. Then what happened? Did you go back to school? Did you --

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- get married? How did you get to Delaware?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Okay. Well, I -- Yes. I did -- I was fortunate, as most of us were fortunate, got the GI Bill. I was able to -- I returned to Harvard. I returned in 1946, June, '46. I came back to the United States, discharged in June of '46 from Fort Dix, same place where I was inducted, and went back home for a few months. And then in September I started back at Harvard with the GI Bill. Amazing thing was that the GI Bill gave us $500 a semester plus, I think, $60 a month living expenses. Harvard cost $400 a semester. We had 100 bucks left over to spend on books, supplies, what have you. Every semester I'd get this case of typewriter paper, pads, pencils, pens, books, you know, just ordinary supplies. I -- It must have been about 40 years later I finally used up all that typewriter paper. But I graduated from Harvard in February. I accelerated. I went a couple of summers. I graduated in February of '49. And I entered the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, got my MBA, went back to live in New York. I got a job working as a personnel/labor relations assistant in Rockefeller Center for the Rockefeller interests there. There were 6,000 employees, including Rockettes and tour guides. But we -- That was -- I did that for about six years, was going to graduate school to get my Ph.D. at NYU. And NYU asked me to set up a career development program for its business and the liberal arts students on the Washington Square Campus, which I did, and it also gave me -- Well, still GI bill was paying my tuition for the Ph.D., but I did that for a few years. And then one of my professors from NYU was with the Ford Foundation, and he asked me to apply for a position in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, with the college placement council. They were setting up a new Ford Foundation project, a three-year project to help develop career programs and improve freely the marketability of graduates of historically black colleges. In those days they were called predominantly Negro colleges. And I got involved through that because through the Rockefellers I had also been involved with the Urban League. One of the Rockefeller brothers was president of the National Urban League. And under that umbrella, I recruited some of the first black architects and accountants and professional black people who were hired by the Rockefellers. But I moved from NYU to this new job, which was supposed to be three years, and it ended up I was 22 years doing that. And I became president of an organization which became known as the Council on Career Development for Minorities. We worked with Hispanic, American Indian, as well as black students in institutions throughout the United States. And then I retired. Well, I had been married after I graduated from Wharton. In '52 I got married, and I lived in Connecticut. (Intercom interruption.)

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Anyway, we were -- I had two daughters, and then somewhere after about 30 years of marriage we got divorced, and I -- about the time that I retired from the CCDM, career development program, I remarried. And I worked for a couple of years in New York with a foundation, Crohn's & Colitis Foundation, as a northeast regional director, which is mainly a fundraising job. And then I retired from that. That's when we came to Delaware in 1990. Both my second wife and I were -- we were living in Jersey, and I was working in Jersey and commuting to New York, very often commuting to New York, because the foundation headquarters was in New York. We were both rather disenchanted, and, well, we had been coming down to Ocean City. We had some friends who have a house in Ocean City, Maryland. And we liked the area, and somehow or other we looked around and found a place in Millsboro, Delaware, which we have been there for now since -- for 14 years. We're very, very happy. She's still working for Easter Seals in Georgetown, and I'm retired.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Thanks. Okay. Now we're going to get into some -- What do you think the history books have left out, if anything, about World War II?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: What have the history books left out about World War II? Well, it's a very -- It's -- There's so many -- I mean, it's a question of what -- There's so many books and things that have been written and television and so forth about World War II. I think the experience of living through it is -- I think people have a hard time -- and I think it's impossible in books and movies or TV to convey this -- the scale of the magnitude, the complete, complete involvement of the country in the war. It was just, I mean, there's nothing that compares ever that experience of World War II in the United States -- and I'm sure all over the world -- but as far as the United States was concerned. For example, you felt bad as a 17-year-old kid getting out of high school being a civilian, walking around, and, you know, everybody is -- uniforms everywhere, uniforms everywhere. I mean, people don't realize that shoes were rationed. Food was rationed. Gasoline was rationed. Tires was rationed. There were blackouts. New York City was dimmed out because the early part of the -- when we were at war, the submarines were sinking ships off here, right off Ocean City. They were silhouetted by the lights. And finally some guy figured out, oh, gee, we've got to dim these lights because they were just sitting ducks. For some reason they didn't even bother to submerge. They sat, and they just fired them with their guns, sank the ships. Anyway, everything was dimmed out. My uncle was a chef at the Rainbow Room in Rockefeller Center, and they closed the Rainbow Room up there on top of what's now the GE building, used to be the RCA building, because of the lights. They couldn't -- They wanted to have the view of the city, but there was no view of the city because everything was dark. Whatever. And they couldn't get the right food and all that. So I think that's the thing, the scale of the total involvement. Everybody was involved or certainly affected by the war and made sacrifices, had to make sacrifices and everything. Like I said, the colleges were running 12 months a year. When I went to Harvard as a civilian, there were only a few hundred civilian students. Most of the dormitories and houses and schools were all involved in training programs for the Army, the Air Force, the Navy. We had Navy WAVES. There were all kinds of training programs. In fact, one of my jobs when I first went to Harvard was as a waiter I was serving the naval communication school. And all these guys were ensigns and lieutenant JGs. They were learning naval communications, I guess, the codes and all of that. And that was just -- Everything was just sort of focused on the war effort.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What do you want the generations to come to know and remember about World War II?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: I think I would like them to know about this kind of a -- not only the sacrifice of the men who got killed and wounded and, like myself, whose life was interrupted, changed, but I think this whole matter of a country that was really very, very much unified and very task oriented and focused. I don't know if this will ever occur again, but it was certainly a unique period in our history.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What major message would you like to leave for generations to come? That could be anything, not even about World War II.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Well, certainly I would think that some of the -- The greatest message is that we should continue to value our system of government, and we should continue to value some of the basic principles, concepts that created this country. And we should try to maintain them at all costs and really not get so bogged down in petty -- what I think political demagoguery, which is so common today. It's really very, very sad, very sad. So I think that's my message. Try to keep focused on the higher things, and don't get bogged down in petty things.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Don't you think, though -- This is off the side of that, but when you just said that, don't you think there was political demagoguery then, but it just wasn't publicized and in your face like it is now?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Well, there is no question that there was demagoguery. I mean, good God, you can look at Huey Long and all the machine politicians, and, yes, absolutely, that's very true, that our country -- As a matter of fact, my father, during the Depression, worked for Mayor Frank Hague out of Jersey City. And he commuted every day from Manhattan to Jersey City. And one of the things, every time he got paid, he had to kick back. A certain percentage of his paycheck went to the guy that went into Frank Hague's machine. He was a chef of the Jersey City Medical Center for the staff, and he was also the private chef of Frank Hague before he got a good job as Stork Club -- chef of the Stork Club in New York. But, yes, there were certainly demagoguery and political shenanigans, but I think it was almost somewhat -- It was so blatant, and it was almost laughable. I mean, when I was at Harvard, the guy that was the mayor of Boston was a man by the name of James Michael Curley. James Michael Curley was sentenced, federal sentence. He was sentenced to jail in Danbury, I believe, and even then he got re-elected while in jail as mayor of Boston. So -- I don't know -- maybe we'll never get away from it, but at least I think we should still remember some of the important things. And certainly people are continually, I guess, fooled by political propaganda or led astray. There's no question James Michael Curley bought his seat. They were putting street lights out in the countryside where there was nobody, but his buddies were contractors, and they hired a lot of guys, and the guys voted.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Pasquale, what do you think? Do you want to do a profile?

sp.speaker: Videographer
sp.p: Yeah, why not.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. What I would like you to do is turn your seat here. Where do you want him to face? That way, right?

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Face the mike, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Just turn profile. There you go, right there.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Is that all right?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. We don't have to talk.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Just going to focus on your beautiful profile.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Andre G. Beaumont
sp.p: All rightee. (Interview concluded)
